I made the following comment in /v/MeanwhileOnReddit (a very entertaining subverse) and I'd like to discuss it. On the topic of worrying about mods here becoming as censorious as mods/powerusers on Reddit:

I don't think the Reddit mods are inherently bad apples; we don't have to worry about them migrating over as much as we should worry about home-grown mods becoming just as bad as the ones on Reddit. I think the problem is endemic to the system, and the only way to prevent it is to experiment with checks and balances that prevent mods from becoming powerusers. Reddit, being a well-established entity with corporate owners, is very unlikely to do anything but allow itself to maintain the status quo with a minimum of experimentation. They're entrenched and have little motivation to fix these problems, unless they have especially good foresight and exceptional power to steer their momentum.

Voat, however, is in a position to address this issue now, not try to struggle with one arm behind its back once it becomes popular. Reddit is teaching us what happens with their model, and we can brainstorm and fix it on Voat today.

How about the following suggestions:

Subverses that are non-default are permitted to establish an "anything-goes" moderation approach, but ones that wish to become defaults must conform to policies that protect free speech and prevent powerusers. Such as:

  1. A system for default subverses where deletions of frontpaged posts (a large number of net upvotes and comments) require mod discussion and a majority mod approval process. The discussion is automatically made public in the event they vote to delete it.

  2. Every subverse has a /deleted section which restores all deleted content--with the exception of doxxing or breaking site-wild rules. No more relying on bots to scrape and post deleted topics

  3. Every subverse has a /rejected section for deleted content that was very popular. Whereas /deleted would be for everything (that wasn't a side-wide rule violation), /rejected would be a /top but for deleted posts

  4. Deletions marked by the mods for doxxing or site-wide rule violations are audited by the admins from time to time, and abuses that statistically vary from the average error rate result in the revocation of a subverse's default status. These audits are made public every quarter.

  5. Mods may only moderate a limited number of default subverses. Three, perhaps? Only one mod account per IP address.

  6. All subverses display a metric called "deletion ratio," showing how frequently that community deletes content vs. other subverses, normalized for traffic/posting rates. A high ratio also doesn't necessarily indicate a bad thing: it just shows that the community is more curated than others.

  7. Default subverses' modmails are anonymized and made public after a month, and any discussion that indicates mods should talk outside of modmail (IRC, email) results in the revocation of their default status.

  8. No deletions without filling out an explanation field. Deleted posts have a sticky area at the top of the comments where a meta-discussion is automatically initiated when the deletion is made.
